key_idea: Split the polynomial into three parts. A rescaled Rudin–Shapiro cosine part is large except on a few short, well-separated intervals, which a Taylor/divided-difference argument controls. On those intervals an odd sine part takes over: it is built as a discrepancy-theory rounding (via a Spencer/Lovett–Meka partial colouring) of a Fourier approximation to a ±1 step function supported there.
reason: The architecture is very clever: combine Rudin–Shapiro structure with Spencer-type discrepancy rounding so that the cosine and sine parts cover each other's weak spots. This explains why flat Littlewood polynomials exist. But the execution leans on many explicit-constant lemmas (derivative bounds, divided differences, Dirichlet-kernel integral estimates, Taylor-expansion rounding at net points), so the elegant core sits under substantial technical bookkeeping.
